title: Practice Makes Something

pages.text:
*From the Dropout Club Handbook, Rule 7: Practice makes... something. Not always perfect.*

Toby stood in the center of the shed, holding a thick textbook open like a map of a place he had never been.

"I have deduced," he said, adjusting his gold-rimmed glasses, "that if I say 'Extinguish,' the light turns on. If I say 'Illuminate,' it goes out. It is consistent. It is beautiful. It is entirely wrong."

He snapped his fingers. The lamp above their heads did not turn on. Instead, the window shutters slammed shut with a crack that shook dust from the rafters.

"Consistent," Marnie said, picking a piece of dried flower petal out of her copper hair.

Lulu tried next. She aimed her wand at the pot-bellied stove. "Float," she whispered. A single lavender sock, smelling faintly of regret, drifted up and stuck to the ceiling.

Bunt, who was holding the textbook like a lectern, suddenly sneezed. It was not a normal sneeze. It was a weather event. A blizzard of paper pages erupted from his nose, swirling around the room until the shed looked like it had been attacked by a very literary snowstorm.

The teapot on the table, which Marnie had been trying to charm into a frog, had already succeeded in becoming a frog. Then, because Marnie’s magic was a bit like a cat with a butterfly, the frog turned into a wheel of cheddar cheese.

"Practice makes something," Toby said, watching the cheese roll under the stove. "Not always perfect."
pages.image: Inside a cluttered garden shed, a large grey-green troll with moss hair sneezes a cloud of paper pages, while a girl in a green cloak looks at a cheddar cheese on the floor and a boy with glasses stares at a floating sock.

pages.text:
Toby fetched a piece of chalk. He sketched a grid on the back wall. He labeled the top "Progress," using the same dry tone he reserved for words like "disaster."

Marnie’s column was a sad little stack of errors: three fish, one duck, two mice, and a wheel of cheddar. It was still hiding under the stove, judging by the pungent smell drifting up. Lulu’s column featured a single, massive number: 212. Two hundred and twelve socks. None of them a pair. All of them lavender.

In Toby’s section, the "Correct Spells" box held a lonely zero. The "Opposite Spells" list ran long and neat. It included a door that opened when commanded to close. It also included a bowl of water that curdled into dry sand. Bunt’s entry was simply: 31 Sneezes.

"We are excellent at being wrong," Lulu said softly. She eyed the sock pile that now towered over her head. "And miserable at being right. I’m sorry, scoreboard."

The scoreboard did not apologize. It just sat there, chalky and quiet. It held their failures up for inspection like a very confused museum exhibit. Marnie felt a strange prickle in her chest. It wasn’t quite pride. It was more like the feeling of finding a loose tooth under your pillow, except the tooth was made of chalk and the pillow was a wall.

"Same time tomorrow?" Toby asked.

"Obviously," Bunt replied. He wiped his nose with a handkerchief the size of a tablecloth.
pages.image: A chalkboard in a shed displaying a list: Marnie with icons of fish, duck, mice, cheese; Lulu with a large pile of socks; Toby with a zero; Bunt with the number 31; four children looking at the list with mixed emotions.

pages.text:
The shout came from the lane, sharp and high-pitched.

"NOT THE SPONGES!"

Marnie’s head snapped toward the window. Through the dusty glass, she saw a broom. It was the sturdy Dimblewick bakery delivery broom, its bristles worn thin, flying. It was not floating; it was towing a wooden cart full to the brim with cream buns, golden and glistening.

Mrs. Humphreys was running after it. She was a small woman covered in so much white flour that she looked like a cloud that had decided to take a walk. Her apron whipped behind her, and her face was a mask of pure panic.

"Stop it! Stop the buns!" she yelled, waving her rolling pin.

The broom did not stop. It galloped down the hill, the wheels of the cart spinning so fast they were blurs, while the buns bounced inside like a golden avalanche waiting to happen.

"Oh dear," Lulu said.

"Oh my," Bunt replied.

Marnie grabbed her wand, and Toby grabbed his. Bunt grabbed a biscuit from his pocket, just in case. Then the four of them were out the door, running down the slope toward the chaos.
pages.image: A wooden broomstick flying through the air, towing a cart full of golden buns, while a small woman in a white apron chases it down a hillside lane, her arms flailing and flour puffing behind her.

pages.text:
They reached the bend just as the broom did, the cart wobbling like a ship in a storm. Marnie raised her wand, not knowing what to do, so she did what she always did. She aimed.

Toby stepped forward, his brown lace-up shoes squeaking on the gravel. "Fly," he said, his voice calm and precise.

Because Toby’s magic works backwards, the broom instantly remembered it was a stick. It stopped dead. The momentum, however, did not.

Lulu didn't think. She grabbed a pile of socks from her hoodie pocket and threw them. A mountain of lavender wool hit the road. The wheels gripped the soft fabric. The buns bounced once, twice, and settled into the wool, cushioned and safe.

Bunt reached out with one massive hand and caught the back of the cart. He stopped it with a gentle *thud*.

Marnie, still aiming, felt a tingle in her wand. She tried to calm the broom, but it slipped. A puff of purple smoke hit the wheel. The wood vanished. In its place sat a large, round wheel of cheddar cheese.

It was slippery. It was perfect. The cart glided to a stop, silent and smooth, the cheese wheel acting as an excellent, edible brake.
pages.image: A four-wheeled cart with one wheel replaced by a round wheel of cheese, stopping on a grassy lane; a girl in a green cloak looks surprised, a boy with glasses looks relieved, a troll holds the cart, and a pile of lavender socks cushions a box of buns.

pages.text:
Mrs. Humphreys stood over the cart, rolling pin poised. She surveyed the cheese wheel, the mountain of socks, and the four of them.

"Well," she said, wiping flour from her forehead. "That was either very clever or very lucky."

"Probably both," Marnie replied.

Mrs. Humphreys reached into the cart and pulled out a seed cake, still warm. She pressed it into Marnie’s hands, then handed over a sack of buns. "For the... club," she said.

They sat on the bakery wall, the sun warming their faces. The cheese wheel was gone, consumed by Bunt in a single crunch. The socks remained on the road, a lavender trail leading away from the bakery.

Toby sat with his knees pulled up to his chest. He looked at Marnie, then Lulu, then Bunt. "That was..." he started, then stopped. He adjusted his glasses. "That was all of us."

Marnie smiled. It was a small smile, but it reached her eyes. She didn’t need to say anything. She didn’t need to be perfect. She just needed to be there, with the cheese, the socks, the sneezes, and the boy who made things do the opposite of what they should.

Behind them, at the top of the lane, a boy in a royal-blue blazer watched. He held a golden notebook. He did not smile. He wrote something down, then closed the book.
pages.image: Four children sitting on a low stone wall eating buns and cake, smiling at each other; in the background, a boy with perfect golden hair in a blue blazer stands at the top of a hill watching them, holding a small golden notebook.
